title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Introduction
Clustering is a central technique in unsupervised machine learning, used to reveal natural groupings within complex datasets where class labels are unknown. Among its methods, K-Means clustering remains widely applied for its simplicity, scalability, and interpretability (Mohd Talib, Abd Majid, and Sahran 2023). The algorithm partitions data into (k) groups based on similarity, minimizing within-cluster variance while increasing separation between clusters. This structure is valuable when the goal is understanding rather than prediction, such as comparing institutions by quantitative indicators of performance, resources, and access.
In higher education research, cluster analysis has long been used to explore structural and performance diversity across institutions (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005). This approach makes it possible to move beyond broad categorical labels and examine measurable dimensions such as outcomes, funding, and enrollment scale. A two-stage framework that combines factor analysis with clustering has also been proposed to derive empirically grounded institutional types (Elam 2016).
Standardized data and documentation have increased the reliability of these methods (National Center for Education Statistics 2023). Best practices for merging and cleaning educational datasets emphasize reproducibility and schema consistency in large-scale analysis (Kelchen 2019). Together, these sources point to the value of structured, data-driven methods in institutional research. The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), maintained by the National Center for Education Statistics, provides the standardized foundation for this type of large-scale institutional analysis. IPEDS collects consistent and comparable data on U.S. colleges and universities, making it a central source for empirical studies that analyze institutional differences through quantitative modeling.
Hybrid models further advance peer identification by pairing quantitative clustering with expert validation, improving interpretability and practical use (Texas Association for Institutional Research 2022). This balance between algorithmic structure and contextual review supports robust benchmarking and decision-making.
The present study applies K-Means clustering to IPEDS data to identify data-driven groupings of postsecondary institutions based on financial, academic, and outcome indicators. The objective is to uncover underlying institutional profiles that describe how U.S. colleges and universities align or differ in measurable ways, offering a transparent and scalable framework for understanding institutional diversity (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005; National Center for Education Statistics 2023; Elam 2016).

1) Grocery stores in Kenya (customer segmentation)
Title: Application of K-Means Clustering for Customer Segmentation in Grocery Stores in Kenya
Link: https://ijstm.inarah.co.id/index.php/ijstm/article/view/1024
Summary:
This study groups grocery shoppers using K Means on transaction and basic demographic data. It matters because smaller stores still need simple ways to understand buying patterns and target customers better. The authors cleaned the data, tested cluster counts with the elbow method, and profiled the groups by behavior. The results gave clear segments that stores can use for marketing and stocking, though the setup is limited by the data available to small shops.

2) Department store case (user profiling)
Title: Applying K-Means Clustering for User Profiling in Retail: A Department Store Case Study
Link: https://www.atlantis-press.com/article/125992628.pdf
Summary:
This paper uses membership and transaction data from a department store to build shopper profiles with K Means. It’s important because simple, interpretable clusters help teams design targeted offers and loyalty programs. The authors picked the number of clusters using the elbow method and the Calinski–Harabasz index, then described each group in plain terms. It shows a straightforward pipeline from retail data to actionable profiles, but it does not bring in extra context like demographics.

3) Online retail with weighted K Means (RFM)
Title: Customer analytics for online retailers using weighted K-Means and RFM analysis
Link: https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2094/679b670242e4177670b839fd7736fc454afa.pdf
Summary:
This study tries to improve customer segmentation by combining RFM features (recency, frequency, monetary) with a weighted K Means variant. The goal is cleaner groups that help with targeting and retention. Using a large UK online retail dataset, the authors built RFM, compared standard vs weighted K Means, and evaluated with silhouette scores. Weighted K Means did better (about 0.40 vs 0.30), but using only RFM can miss other behavior, so the view of the customer is still limited.

4) Comparing clustering algorithms on UK retail data
Title: An Exploration of Clustering Algorithms for Customer Segmentation in the UK Retail Market
Link: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.04103
Summary:
This paper compares several clustering methods for retail segmentation using RFM features, including K Means, Gaussian Mixture Models, DBSCAN, BIRCH, and agglomerative clustering. It matters because the choice of algorithm changes how useful the groups are for marketing and planning. The results showed GMM scored highest on silhouette (around 0.80) in this setup, with K Means and others lower. The dataset is mostly transactions, so the clusters do not include extra context like demographics or browsing.

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Methods
This study applies the K-Means clustering algorithm to group U.S. higher education institutions into data-driven segments based on scale, resources, access, and outcomes. The process follows the standard Lloyd–Forgy heuristic for iterative centroid-based optimization, as described in the literature on higher education clustering and institutional classification (Lloyd 1982).

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Analysis and Results

Data Exploration and Visualization

Dataset Overview
This study uses institutional-level data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) for the 2023 collection year (2023–2024 cycle). IPEDS collects standardized information from all U.S. postsecondary institutions participating in federal financial aid programs, covering public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit sectors.
The following survey components were used and merged on the key UNITID:

HD2023 — Institutional characteristics (name, control, sector, etc.)
F2223_F1A — Finance (public, GASB)
F2223_F2 — Finance (private nonprofit, FASB)
F2223_F3 — Finance (private for-profit)
EFIA2023 — 12-month instructional activity (source of FTE)
ADM2023 — Admissions (admission rate, tuition; optional in analysis)
OM2023 — Outcome measures (completion/attainment; optional in analysis)

All files were downloaded from the NCES IPEDS Data Center.



Variable Selection and Preparation
To represent institutional scale, financial capacity, access, and outcomes, variables were drawn from multiple components and aligned by UNITID. Below are the primary fields used in this phase:








Feature Group
Variable (Field)
Description

Total full-time-equivalent enrollment (UG + Grad + DPP if present).

Total revenues (public), total revenues & investment return (nonprofit/for-profit).



INSTR_EXP (F1C011 / F2E011 / F3E011)
Instructional expenses (aligned across control types).



TOT_EXP (F1N07 / F2B02 / F3B02)
Total operating expenses.


Access & Price

Admission rate; in-state tuition/fees (if used).


Outcomes
e.g., OM8_PCT_COMP (OM2023)
8-year outcome/completion measure (if used).




Note: Where variables differ by control type, fields were harmonized to a shared name (e.g., TOT_REV, INSTR_EXP, TOT_EXP). Ratios per FTE are derived after FTE merge.




Data Cleaning and Integration
Finance data from public (F1A), private nonprofit (F2), and private for-profit (F3) files were imported and standardized to total revenue, instructional expense, and total expense. Twelve-month instructional activity (EFIA2023) provided undergraduate, graduate, and total FTE values; reported FTE were preferred, with estimated values as fallback. All monetary values are reported in nominal USD for 2023–24 and not inflation-adjusted.
Tables were merged using left joins on UNITID to preserve coverage. Numeric missing values were left as NA to maintain fidelity with NCES reporting. After filtering to active, degree-granting institutions with valid FTE, the analytic file contains ~6,000 institutions across all three control types.


Code
# ----libraries-------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling / joins / ggplot2
library(janitor)     # clean column names
library(gt)          # summary tables
library(scales)      # formatting helpers
library(GGally)      # quick pair plots (optional)
library(corrr)       # correlation summaries (optional)
library(here)        # reproducible relative paths
library(patchwork)   # plot layouts (optional)

# ----paths-----------------------------------------------------------------
data_dir <- here("data")  # change if your files live elsewhere

# ----helper: robust numeric coercion--------------------------------------
numify <- function(x) as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.\\-]", "", as.character(x)))

# ----load core IPEDS components-------------------------------------------
hd  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "HD2023.csv"))   |> clean_names()
adm <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ADM2023.csv"))  |> clean_names()
om  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "OM2023.csv"))   |> clean_names()

# Finance (public / private nonprofit / private for-profit)
f1a <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F1A.csv")) |> clean_names()
f2  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F2.csv"))  |> clean_names()
f3  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F3.csv"))  |> clean_names()

# 12-month instructional activity (FTE source) — treat “.”, etc. as NA
efia <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "EFIA2023.csv"),
                 na = c("", ".", "-", "—", "NA", "N/A")) |> clean_names()

# Student charges (tuition and fees)
ic_ay <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "IC2023.csv"))  |> clean_names()

# Student financial aid (Pell Grant %)
sfa <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "SFA2223.csv"))   |> clean_names()

# Fall retention & student-faculty ratio
ef2023d <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "EF2023D.csv")) |> clean_names()

# ----EFIA -> FTE totals (coerce safely)-----------------------------------
efia <- efia |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("fteug","efteug","ftegd","eftegd","ftedpp")), numify))

efia_fte <- efia |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    fte_ug    = coalesce(fteug,  efteug),
    fte_grad  = coalesce(ftegd,  eftegd),
    fte_dpp   = ftedpp,
    fte_total = coalesce(fteug,  efteug, 0) +
                coalesce(ftegd,  eftegd, 0) +
                coalesce(ftedpp, 0)
  )

# ----finance: align to common names & coerce numeric-----------------------
f1a_fin <- f1a |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("f1d01","f1c011","f1n07")), numify)) |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f1d01,    # Total revenues & other additions (public)
    instr_exp = f1c011,   # Instruction - current year total
    tot_exp   = f1n07,    # Total expenses
    control   = "Public"
  )

f2_fin <- f2 |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("f2d162","f2e011","f2b02")), numify)) |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f2d162,   # Total revenues & investment return - unrestricted
    instr_exp = f2e011,   # Instruction - total amount
    tot_exp   = f2b02,    # Total expenses
    control   = "Private Nonprofit"
  )

f3_fin <- f3 |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("f3d12","f3e011","f3b02")), numify)) |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f3d12,    # Total revenues & investment return
    instr_exp = f3e011,   # Instruction - total amount
    tot_exp   = f3b02,    # Total expenses
    control   = "Private For-Profit"
  )

fin <- bind_rows(f1a_fin, f2_fin, f3_fin)

# ----unified sector handling (robust)--------------------------------------
# 1) Keep finance-derived sector label, drop 'control' to avoid control.x/y later
fin <- fin |>
  mutate(sector_fin = control) |>
  select(-control)

# 2) From HD, build sector label if a numeric 'control' exists; else NA
if ("control" %in% names(hd)) {
  hd <- hd |>
    mutate(
      sector_hd = dplyr::case_match(
        control,
        1 ~ "Public",
        2 ~ "Private Nonprofit",
        3 ~ "Private For-Profit",
        .default = NA_character_
      )
    )
} else {
  hd <- hd |> mutate(sector_hd = NA_character_)
}

# ----tuition, Pell, retention, stufacr (robust numeric)-------------------
ic_sel <- ic_ay |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("tuition1")), numify)) |>
  transmute(unitid, tuition1)

sfa_sel <- sfa |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("pgrnt_p")), numify)) |>
  transmute(unitid, pct_pell = pgrnt_p)

ef_ret <- ef2023d |>
  mutate(across(any_of(c("ret_pcf","ret_pcp","stufacr")), numify)) |>
  transmute(unitid, ret_pcf, ret_pcp, stufacr)

# ----merge all components (single clean 'sector')--------------------------
ipeds <- hd |>
  left_join(fin,      by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(efia_fte, by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(ic_sel,   by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(sfa_sel,  by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(ef_ret,   by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(adm,      by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(om,       by = "unitid") |>
  mutate(
    sector = dplyr::coalesce(sector_hd, sector_fin),
    sector = factor(sector,
                    levels = c("Public", "Private Nonprofit", "Private For-Profit"))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(unitid), !is.na(fte_total), fte_total > 0) |>
  distinct(unitid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    rev_per_fte    = tot_rev   / fte_total,
    instr_exp_fte  = instr_exp / fte_total,
    exp_per_fte    = tot_exp   / fte_total,
    retention_rate = coalesce(ret_pcf, ret_pcp)  # prefer full-time, else part-time
  )

# ----quick composition summary (uses clean 'sector')-----------------------
ipeds |>
  summarise(
    total_institutions = n(),
    public_share       = mean(sector == "Public",             na.rm = TRUE),
    nonprofit_share    = mean(sector == "Private Nonprofit",  na.rm = TRUE),
    forprofit_share    = mean(sector == "Private For-Profit", na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = 2:4, decimals = 1)

Modeling and Results
This section presents the analytical process and results of applying the K-Means clustering algorithm to institutional data from IPEDS.
While the Methods section established the theoretical foundations and variable design, this section focuses on how the model was implemented, how the optimal number of clusters was determined, and what structural patterns emerged across institutional segments.


Data Preparation for Modeling
Prior to clustering, all selected quantitative features were standardized using z-score normalization to ensure comparability across scales.
The final modeling dataset included institutions with valid and complete entries for key financial, access, and outcome metrics:

REV_PER_FTE: Revenue per full-time equivalent student

INSTR_EXP_FTE: Instructional expense per FTE

TUITION1: In-state undergraduate tuition and fees

OM8_PCT_COMP: 8-year student completion rate

RETENTION_RATE: First-year retention (full-time preferred; part-time if missing)

Each row of the modeling dataset corresponds to a unique institution (UNITID), and each column represents a standardized feature describing resources, affordability, or student outcomes.
To reduce the influence of extreme but valid outliers—such as very large public university systems or small proprietary colleges—variables were Winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles, preserving their presence while mitigating skew in centroid placement.




Determining the Optimal Number of Clusters
Selecting an appropriate number of clusters, ( k ), is a key decision in K-Means because it determines the level of segmentation and affects both interpretability and model stability.
To guide this choice, two internal validation techniques were applied:

Elbow Method (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares, WCSS) — identifies the point at which adding more clusters produces diminishing improvements in compactness.

Silhouette Analysis — evaluates how well each institution fits within its assigned cluster relative to neighboring clusters.

Together, these diagnostics balance parsimony (using fewer, more interpretable clusters) and stability (ensuring clusters are coherent and well separated).
Both methods pointed toward ( k ) as a stable and interpretable solution.


Code
library(cluster)

# Prepare modeling matrix
X <- vis_df |>
  select(rev_per_fte, instr_exp_fte, tuition1, om8_pct_comp, retention_rate) |>
  drop_na() |>
  scale()

# --- Elbow ---------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(2024)
wcss <- map_dbl(1:10, ~ kmeans(X, centers = .x, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss)
elbow_df <- tibble(k = 1:10, wcss = wcss)

ggplot(elbow_df, aes(k, wcss)) +
  geom_line(color = "#4682B4", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#B2182B") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.25, y = max(wcss)*0.8, label = "Elbow ≈ 4", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 7. Elbow Method for Optimal k",
    subtitle = "Elbow point suggests diminishing returns beyond k = 4",
    x = "Number of clusters (k)",
    y = "Total Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)





Elbow and Silhouette Analysis for Optimal k




Code
# --- Silhouette -----------------------------------------------------
silhouette_scores <- map_dbl(2:10, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  ss <- silhouette(km$cluster, dist(X))
  mean(ss[, 3])
})

sil_df <- tibble(k = 2:10, silhouette = silhouette_scores)

ggplot(sil_df, aes(k, silhouette)) +
  geom_line(color = "#4B9CD3", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#E66101") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.3, y = max(silhouette_scores)*0.97, label = "Peak ≈ 4", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 8. Silhouette Analysis for Cluster Cohesion and Separation",
    subtitle = "Peak silhouette width supports k = 4",
    x = "Number of clusters (k)",
    y = "Average silhouette width"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

Cluster Segmentation Narratives

Cluster 1 — Broad-Access, Lower-Resource Institutions
This segment tends to include institutions with lower tuition, limited instructional spending, and below-average completion rates. They are often regional, commuter-serving, or open-access colleges where affordability is high but resource constraints may affect instructional capacity and student support. Retention is modest, indicating challenges in sustaining student persistence.


Cluster 2 — Moderately Resourced Institutions with Balanced Outcomes
Cluster 2 exhibits mid-range tuition, moderate spending, and solid student outcomes. These institutions represent a balanced “middle tier” of higher education, often including regional publics and private nonprofits with stable performance metrics despite less intense resource levels than elite institutions.


Cluster 3 — High-Tuition, High-Resource Institutions
Institutions in this segment show substantially higher tuition, significant instructional investment, and correspondingly high completion and retention rates. This profile aligns with selective universities and well-resourced private institutions operating under a “high input, high output” model.


Cluster 4 — Low-Tuition but Strong-Outcome Institutions
This segment includes institutions maintaining lower-than-average tuition yet attaining strong completion and retention rates. Often efficient public institutions or community colleges, these schools demonstrate that strong student outcomes do not universally require high expenditure levels.

Conclusion
This project used K-Means clustering on IPEDS data to break institutions into groups based on resources, affordability, and student success. The variables were standardized and Winsorized to keep outliers from pulling the model around. Both the Elbow method and the Silhouette scores pointed toward four clusters, and that setup ended up giving the clearest and most stable structure.
The final groups showed four different types of institutions. One group captured broad access schools that operate with fewer resources and see lower retention and completion. Another group sat in the middle, with moderate spending, moderate tuition, and steady outcomes. A third group represented well funded schools with high tuition and strong performance. The last group stood out because they kept tuition low while still producing solid retention and completion. That pattern shows that resources matter, but they are not the whole story when it comes to student outcomes.
The diagnostic checks backed this up. The boxplots showed clear separation across each variable, and the PCA plot showed four distinct groups when the data was compressed into two components. PCA was only used to visualize structure, but it made the spacing between clusters easier to see.
Overall, the results show that a small, focused set of metrics is enough to reveal real structure in the higher education landscape. These segments can help with peer grouping, benchmarking, and conversations about funding and equity. Future work could bring in more variables, test other clustering approaches, or look at how student demographics and program mix change the picture. Even with the limited scope here, the model gives a clear and useful view of how institutions differ across the system.

title: Capstone: K-Means Clustering on Retail Data
text:
In retail, not all customers are the same. Some shop often and spend a lot, while others buy less or shop only occasionally. Treating all customers the same can lead to missed opportunities. K-Means clustering helps retailers by grouping customers with similar behaviors, such as spending levels or shopping frequency. These groups can then be targeted with the right offers, discounts, and services. Beyond customers, K-Means can also be used in inventory management, dividing products into fast-moving, stable, or slow-moving categories to reduce waste and improve stock planning.
For this project we are working with a retail dataset that holds transactional records with details on purchases and spending patterns. Our plan is to clean and prepare the data, choose features that capture customer and product behavior, and then apply K-Means clustering to see how the groups form. From there we will evaluate the clusters and describe them in clear terms, showing how the results can guide decisions for marketing, promotions, and inventory.

PDF Link – Biometrics
Forgy (1965) is one of the earliest pieces that explains how to run clustering in multivariate settings, including what later got called the Forgy initialization for K Means. The paper talks through the balance between squeezing out statistical efficiency and keeping the results readable. A lot of the choices in this project about how clusters are initialized and evaluated trace back to this foundation.

PDF Link – Springer
Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt (2005) show how cluster analysis has been used to study diversity and performance patterns across colleges. They point out that clustering can reveal similarities and gaps that the standard categories hide, especially when you stack financial and outcome data together. They also go over variable choice, scaling, and validation, which feeds directly into the structure of this capstone.

Data Clustering: 50 Years Beyond K Means
PDF Link – Pattern Recognition Letters
Jain (2010) looks back over five decades of clustering research. K Means is the anchor point, but the paper compares it to other algorithms and distance choices. It highlights what works about K Means, like its speed and clarity, and also where it struggles, like odd shaped clusters and sensitivity to initialization. This context supports using K Means here while being honest about its limits with institutional data.

It explains the iterative assignment and update steps and shows that the objective will always drop even though the algorithm can land in local minima. Modeling and Results
This section presents the analytical process and results of applying the K-Means clustering algorithm to institutional data from IPEDS. While the Methods section laid out the modeling framework and variable design, this section focuses on how the model was implemented, how the optimal number of clusters was chosen, and what structural patterns emerged across institutional segments.


Data Preparation for Modeling
Prior to clustering, all selected quantitative features were standardized using z-score normalization to ensure comparability across scales. The final modeling dataset included institutions with valid and complete entries for key financial, access, and outcome metrics:

REV_PER_FTE: revenue per full-time equivalent student

INSTR_EXP_FTE: instructional expense per FTE

TUITION1: in-state undergraduate tuition and fees

OM8_PCT_COMP: 8-year student completion rate

RETENTION_RATE: first-year retention (full-time preferred; part-time if missing)

Each row of the modeling dataset corresponds to a unique institution (UNITID), and each column represents a standardized feature describing resources, affordability, or student outcomes. To reduce the influence of extreme but valid outliers (for example, very large public systems or small proprietary colleges), variables were Winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles. This preserves these institutions in the data while limiting their impact on centroid placement.



Determining the Optimal Number of Clusters
Selecting an appropriate number of clusters, (k), is a key decision in K-Means because it determines the level of segmentation and affects both interpretability and stability. To guide this choice, two internal validation techniques were applied:

Elbow method (within-cluster sum of squares, WCSS) — used to identify the point where adding more clusters yields diminishing improvements in compactness.

Silhouette analysis — used to evaluate how well each institution fits within its assigned cluster relative to neighboring clusters.

Together, these diagnostics balance parsimony (fewer, more interpretable clusters) and stability (coherent and well-separated clusters). Both methods pointed toward (k ) as a stable and interpretable solution.

  select(rev_per_fte, instr_exp_fte, tuition1, om8_pct_comp, retention_rate) |>

Cluster 3 — High-Tuition, High-Resource Institutions
Institutions in this segment show substantially higher tuition, significant instructional investment, and correspondingly high completion and retention rates. This profile aligns with selective universities and well-resourced private institutions that operate on a “high input, high output” model.


Cluster 4 — Low-Tuition but Strong-Outcome Institutions
This segment includes institutions that maintain lower-than-average tuition yet achieve strong completion and retention rates. Often efficient public institutions or community colleges, these schools show that strong student outcomes do not always require high expenditure levels.



Visualizing Cluster Structure in Feature Space
To visualize how institutions separate in high-dimensional space, the standardized modeling matrix was projected into two components using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). PCA was not used for model fitting; instead, it provides a compact visualization that shows whether clusters form coherent regions. PC1 is primarily associated with overall resource intensity, and PC2 captures variation related to affordability and outcomes.

Exploratory Data Analysis

Data Exploration and Visualization

Dataset Overview
This study uses institutional-level data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) for the 2023 collection year (2023–2024 cycle). IPEDS collects standardized information from all U.S. postsecondary institutions that participate in federal financial aid programs, covering the public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit sectors.
The following survey components were used and merged on the key UNITID:

HD2023 — Institutional characteristics (name, control, sector, etc.)
F2223_F1A — Finance (public, GASB)
F2223_F2 — Finance (private nonprofit, FASB)
F2223_F3 — Finance (private for-profit)
EFIA2023 — 12-month instructional activity (source of FTE)
ADM2023 — Admissions (admission rate, tuition; used selectively)
OM2023 — Outcome measures (completion/attainment; used selectively)

All files were downloaded from the NCES IPEDS Data Center.



Variable Selection and Preparation
To represent institutional scale, financial capacity, access, and outcomes, variables were drawn from multiple components and aligned by UNITID. The main fields used are summarized below:

Variable (Field)

Total full-time-equivalent enrollment (UG + Grad + DPP if present).

Total revenues (public), total revenues and investment return (nonprofit/for-profit).



INSTR_EXP (F1C011 / F2E011 / F3E011)
Instructional expenses (aligned across control types).

Total operating expenses.

Admission rate; in-state tuition and fees.

8-year outcome/completion measure.



Where variables differed by control type, fields were harmonized to shared names (for example, TOT_REV, INSTR_EXP, TOT_EXP). Ratios per FTE were computed after merging FTE data.



Data Cleaning and Integration
Finance data from public (F1A), private nonprofit (F2), and private for-profit (F3) files were imported and mapped to total revenue, instructional expense, and total expense. Twelve-month instructional activity (EFIA2023) provided undergraduate, graduate, and total FTE values; reported FTE were preferred, with estimated values as fallback. Monetary values are reported in nominal USD for 2023–24 and are not inflation-adjusted.
Tables were merged with left joins on UNITID to preserve coverage. Numeric missing values were left as NA in order to stay consistent with NCES reporting. title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Conclusion
This project used K-Means clustering on IPEDS data to break institutions into groups based on resources, affordability, and student success. The variables were standardized and Winsorized to keep outliers from pulling the model around. Both the Elbow method and the Silhouette scores pointed toward four clusters, and that setup ended up giving the clearest and most stable structure.
The final groups showed four different types of institutions. One group captured broad access schools that operate with fewer resources and see lower retention and completion. Another group sat in the middle, with moderate spending, moderate tuition, and steady outcomes. A third group represented well-funded schools with high tuition and strong performance. The last group stood out because they kept tuition low while still producing solid retention and completion. That pattern shows that resources matter, but they are not the whole story when it comes to student outcomes.
The diagnostic checks backed this up. The boxplots showed clear separation across each variable, and the PCA plot showed four distinct groups when the data was compressed into two components. PCA was only used to visualize structure, but it made the spacing between clusters easier to see.
Overall, the results show that a small, focused set of metrics is enough to reveal real structure in the higher education landscape. These segments can help with peer grouping, benchmarking, and conversations about funding and equity. Future work could bring in more variables, test other clustering approaches, or look at how student demographics and program mix change the picture. Even with the limited scope here, the model gives a clear and useful view of how institutions differ across the system.

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Objective and Notation
Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) be the standardized feature matrix, where each row represents an institution and each column represents a numeric feature such as revenue per FTE, tuition, or completion rate. The goal of K Means is to partition \(n\) observations into \(k\) clusters \(C = \{C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k\}\) and to estimate centroids \(\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_k\) that minimize the within cluster sum of squares (WCSS):
\[
\min_{C} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x_j \in C_i} \lVert x_j - \mu_i \rVert^2
\]
For a fixed cluster assignment, the centroid for cluster \(i\) is the mean of the observations in \(C_i\):
\[
\mu_i = \frac{1}{|C_i|} \sum_{x_j \in C_i} x_j
\]
This optimization problem is NP hard, so this capstone uses the Lloyd Forgy routine (Lloyd 1982) to approximate a solution through alternating assignment and update st


Lloyd’s Algorithm (Assignment and Update)
The algorithm alternates between two phases until it converges:

Assignment step
Each observation is assigned to the nearest cluster centroid based on Euclidean distance: \[
C_i^{(t)} = \{x_j : \|x_j - \mu_i^{(t)}\|^2 \leq \|x_j - \mu_r^{(t)}\|^2,\ \forall r \in \{1, \ldots, k\}\}
\]
Update step
After assignments, centroids are updated to reflect the mean of their current members: \[
\mu_i^{(t+1)} = \frac{1}{|C_i^{(t)}|} \sum_{x_j \in C_i^{(t)}} x_j
\]

The process repeats until there is minimal change in cluster assignments or centroid locations between iterations (Lloyd 1982).



Feature Scaling and Preprocessing
Because IPEDS variables differ in magnitude and measurement units (for example, tuition in USD, completion rates as percentages, and revenue per FTE in dollars), all continuous numeric variables were standardized using z-score normalization prior to clustering (Lloyd 1982; Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005):
\[
z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}
\]
where ({x}) is the sample mean and (s) is the sample standard deviation. This ensures that each variable contributes on a comparable scale to the Euclidean distances used in K-Means clustering (Lloyd 1982).
Categorical fields, such as institutional control type, were not standardized. Instead, they were reserved for post-cluster interpretation and comparison.
To lessen the impact of extreme but valid institutional profiles (for example, very large public systems or small for-profit colleges), Winsorization was applied to cap values beyond the 1st and 99th percentiles. This preserves the presence of these institutions while limiting their leverage on centroid placement and cluster boundaries (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005).



Implementation Procedure
K-Means was implemented using R’s base stats::kmeans() function with multiple random initializations (nstart = 25) to reduce sensitivity to initial centroid placement. To ensure reproducibility, all random seeds were fixed using set.seed(2024).
Cluster inputs included:

REV_PER_FTE (revenue per full-time equivalent)
INSTR_EXP_FTE (instructional expenses per FTE)
TUITION1 (in-state undergraduate tuition)
OM8_PCT_COMP (8-year completion rate)
RET_PCF (retention rate, full-time; part-time as fallback)

The optimal number of clusters (k) was not pre-specified in this section. It is evaluated empirically in the Modeling and Results section using the Elbow method and Silhouette analysis, following (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005; Texas Association for Institutional Research 2022).



Justification of Method
K-Means was selected for its interpretability and computational efficiency on medium-dimensional data. Prior studies in higher education analytics have shown that unsupervised clustering can reveal institutional typologies that traditional classifications overlook (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005; National Center for Education Statistics 2023; Mohd Talib, Abd Majid, and Sahran 2023; Elam 2016). This approach supports empirical grouping based on shared performance and resource characteristics, providing a basis for benchmarking and peer comparison (Kelchen 2019).



Cluster Validation and Model Evaluation
To ensure that groupings derived from K-Means were both stable and interpretable, multiple internal validation techniques were applied. Because K-Means requires the number of clusters (k) to be specified in advance, choosing an appropriate (k) is a key step that affects both interpretability and robustness (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005; Texas Association for Institutional Research 2022).

Elbow Method (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares)
The Elbow method evaluates the total within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) across a range of (k) values:
\[
WCSS(k) = \min_C \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x_j \in C_i} \|x_j - \mu_i\|^2
\]
As (k) increases, WCSS decreases because cluster radii shrink. The optimal (k) is typically chosen at the “elbow” point: the inflection where additional clusters yield diminishing reductions in WCSS. This heuristic balances compact clusters with a parsimonious number of groups.


Silhouette Analysis
Silhouette analysis was used to complement the Elbow approach and assess how well each institution fits within its assigned cluster compared to neighboring clusters (Mohd Talib, Abd Majid, and Sahran 2023). The Silhouette coefficient for observation (i) is
\[
s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max[a(i), b(i)]}
\]
where

(a(i)) is the average distance between (i) and all other points in its cluster (cohesion),

(b(i)) is the minimum average distance between (i) and points in the nearest neighboring cluster (separation).

Values range from (-1) to (1), with higher scores indicating better separation and cohesion. The average Silhouette width was computed across all institutions for each candidate (k), and the value of (k) with the highest mean silhouette was treated as the most stable partition.


Model Stability and Reproducibility
To reduce randomness from centroid initialization, the clustering routine was run with multiple random starts (nstart = 25) and a fixed seed (set.seed(2024)), following best practices for reproducible analysis (Kelchen 2019). This helps ensure that the resulting segmentation is not an artifact of a single random state.


Summary
This validation framework combines geometric compactness (Elbow method) and structural separation (Silhouette coefficient) to justify the final number of clusters. The choice of (k) and the interpretation of the resulting segments are presented in the following sections.
